title: Sita
hook: the war is won, and Rama speaks harshly to Sita in front of everyone; she answers him, then asks for a fire

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sita in the ashoka grove: a blade of grass between her and Ravana, and a no to Hanuman's offer of a ride home. Did you set down one small boundary? Day one thousand three hundred thirty-one.

The war is over. Ravana is dead. Sita is brought out in front of the whole army, and the reunion the story has been moving toward doesn't come. In Valmiki's sixth book, Rama speaks to her coldly, in public. He says, in paraphrase, that he fought to clear his name and his family's, and that she may go wherever she likes. It's a hard scene to read. Today isn't about defending it or explaining it away. It's about the woman who has to answer it, and what she says.
screen: `THE WAR IS OVER.` → `NO REUNION, A COLD SPEECH.` → `WHAT SITA SAYS BACK.`

segments.voice: Sita doesn't stay silent. She wipes her tears and speaks, and Valmiki gives her a full answer. Here it is in paraphrase. Why do you speak to me like this, she asks, the way a common man speaks to a common woman? What was in my power, my heart, was always yours. What was not in my power, my body seized by force, was not my doing. If you meant to give me up, she adds, why didn't you say so when Hanuman came? I would have ended my life then, and spared you a war. Then she turns to Lakshmana and asks him to build a fire. She walks around Rama, faces the flames, and calls on Agni, the god of fire, as her witness, and steps in. The fire god himself rises out of the flames, carrying her, and gives her back to Rama, declaring her faultless. Rama then says he never doubted her, and did this so the world would see. So what do we do with this? The tradition itself has not settled it, and it speaks in more than one voice. Some read the fire as Sita's victory: her truth proven before everyone. Some later retellings, including Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, tell it differently, so that the real Sita was never in Lanka at all. Some readers, and some singers of these songs, simply sit with Sita's hurt and her courage. The lesson here is narrower. In the worst moment of her story, Valmiki gives Sita the clearest voice. She names what was hers and what wasn't. She asks her own question. Then she chooses the fire herself.
screen: `SHE WIPES HER TEARS AND SPEAKS` · `MY HEART WAS ALWAYS YOURS` · `SHE ASKS LAKSHMANA FOR A FIRE` · `THE TRADITION STILL ARGUING`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sort what was yours. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one hard thing that's been laid at your door, fairly or not. Then gently sort it, the way Sita did. What part of it was in your power? Breathe with that. What part was never in your power? Breathe that out, and let it rest where it belongs. No verdict needed. If you pray, you can place both parts before God. The bell holds the time.
Sita. After the war, she answers Rama's cold words, names what was hers and what wasn't, and asks for the fire. Today's word.
Your line: Sita. Today, if blame lands on you, sort it once: what was in your power, and what never was. Tomorrow, another woman of the epics, Draupadi. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Sita's ordeal by fire, the agni pariksha, is retold, staged and debated across Hindu traditions; Valmiki, Tulsidas and folk singers tell it in different ways, and Hindu teachers and readers continue to discuss what it means.

original.note: Sanskrit: fire, and the god of fire. Sita calls on Agni as her witness before stepping into the flames.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sita silently accepts the fire ordeal.
what it means: in Valmiki, she answers Rama's cold words first, then chooses the fire herself.
what a scholar hears: Tulsidas and others retell the scene differently, so the tradition holds more than one Sita in this moment.

notes: A sensitive scene; please review tone carefully. The lesson neither defends nor condemns Rama's words and offers several readings without ranking them.
Sarga numbers follow the vulgate (Yuddha 115–118); the critical edition numbers differ. Confirm.

Yuddha 116: confirm the paraphrase of Sita's answer (speaking like a common man to a common woman; her heart, which was in her power, was his; her body, not in her power, was seized; why not renounce her when Hanuman came, when she would have given up her life). The line about ending her life is in the text; it is reported, not dwelt on.
Confirm Sita circumambulates Rama before entering the fire, and that Agni rises carrying her and declares her pure (Yuddha 118), and Rama's statement that he did it for the world's sake.
Ramcharitmanas: confirm the framing that in Tulsidas the real Sita is placed in the fire before the abduction and a shadow Sita is taken to Lanka (Aranya Kanda). Kept to one sentence.
Original: Agni was likely taught earlier on the path; kept here as the witness Sita calls.
Editor pass: hook's 'the reunion everyone has waited for' reworded to avoid a claim about everyone.
